title: slab-coordinator-and-eviction-prioritizer-to-mitigate-head-fragmentation-and-tail-growth
author: Sofia Patel
release_notes: Introduce slab coordinator and eviction prioritizer that reduce KV fragmentation for MQA/GQA models; improves steady-state throughput and reduces tail latency variability. Safe rollout with runtime flag and canary by model tag.
commits_summary: init: add SlabCoordinator and eviction-prioritizer interfaces
impl: slab occupancy accounting, per-head decay and priority scoring
impl: kernel-router hints to prefer coarse-quant paths for low-prio slabs
tests: microbench for slab eviction and end-to-end perf harness
docs: design notes and rollout playbook
description:
Summary:
This PR implements a SlabCoordinator and an EvictionPrioritizer to address head-asymmetry and tail growth observed in GQA/MQA-capable models (notably Qwen and some Mistral variants). The approach reduces KV-cache fragmentation across attention heads by coordinating eviction decisions at slab granularity and by prioritizing eviction based on head activity, recent kernel path, and model-quirk heuristics.

Motivation:
On production workloads we saw two related issues: (1) uneven head utilization (some heads accumulate long KV prefixes while others are idle) which causes poor packing into slabs and increases memory churn, and (2) tail-heavy growth in Qwen due to gated attention patterns that fill slabs with low-benefit tokens. Existing LRU-like eviction was reactive and noisy across concurrent requests leading to frequent kernel-path fallbacks and microburst latency spikes.

Design:
- SlabCoordinator: maintains lightweight occupancy maps at slab granularity (configurable slab-size, default 64 tokens). It exposes atomic increment/decrement and a snapshot API used by eviction logic. Coordination is per-device and per-queue to avoid global locks.
- EvictionPrioritizer: scores candidate slabs using a composite priority: head_activity_decay (exponential decay with tunable tau), kernel_path_penalty (penalize slabs that recently forced expensive per-head kernels), and model_quirk_boost (rules for Qwen: boost eviction score for gated-attention tail buckets; for Mistral: bias against uneven-head-width slabs). The scoring is bounded and normalized to allow deterministic tie-breaking.
- Kernel-router integration: eviction decisions emit hints consumed by kernel router to prefer compatible quantized or fused kernels for remaining slabs, reducing kernel polymorphism when eviction completes. This reduces runtime overhead from frequent kernel swaps for MQA/GQA models.
- Continuous batching alignment: we add a microbatch alignment step that, when enabled, prefers to evict slabs that best align subsequent requests into contiguous KV ranges to improve continuous batching efficiency.

Implementation notes:
- No global locks: per-worker slab maps use atomic counters and epoch-based reclamation; safe under preemption.
- Runtime flags: feature gate slab_eviction.enabled + two tuning knobs (decay_tau, slab_size) added to runtime config and feature-flags config example included.
- Telemetry: new metrics exported: slab_eviction.score_distribution, slab_compaction_events, slab_fragmentation_ratio; these are surfaced in the Console to aid rollout.

Tests & Results:
- Microbenchmarks (tests/perf/slab_coordinator_bench.cc) simulate head-asymmetric traffic and gated-attention bursts.
- On our internal GQA test-suite with mixed Mistral/Qwen traffic, we saw: median latency -3.8%, p95 tail latency -11.2%, tokens/sec +6.4% in steady-state.
- On Llama-heavy workloads (dense heads) the change is neutral to +2.1% throughput and reduces memory churn.
- A flaky perf test initially regressed by 1.5% under synthetic worst-case; after tuning the decay_tau default the CI perf suite passed on rerun.

Rollout plan:
1) Merge behind feature flag (default off for dedicated customers).
2) Canary to ~5% of traffic for models tagged with 'mq-gqa-enabled' for 48h.
3) Expand canary, monitor slab_fragmentation_ratio and kernel_switch_rate.
4) Graduate to full rollout with auto-tuning of decay_tau if metrics show stable improvement.

Backward compatibility:
- Default behavior unchanged when slab_eviction.enabled=false.
- Kernel hints are advisory; router falls back to current selection if unsupported.

Related work:
- This complements existing KV prefetch/prefill heuristics and continuous batching improvements; it focuses on eviction ordering rather than prefetching. See ENG-2145 for prior notes.

Checklist:
- [x] design doc added (docs/architecture/kv-scheduling.md)
- [x] unit tests + microbench added
- [x] metrics + dashboards instrumented
- [x] rollout runbook included

Small illustrative snippet (eviction score formula):
score = w_activity * (1 - exp(-age / tau)) + w_kernel * kernel_penalty + w_quirk * model_boost
(The actual implementation normalizes weights and clamps score to [0,1])

If enabling for a model and you see increased kernel switch rate, reduce decay_tau by factor of 2 and enable microbatch alignment for that model tag.

Diego Ramirez (2026-02-23): Can we make the model_quirk rules data-driven? Response: added a TODO and Linear ENG-2182 to follow up; kept conservative heuristics for now. Priya Nair (2026-02-24): FLaky perf - please run workload replay; response: replay attached and adjusted default tau (2026-02-25). Final: approved by reviewers (2026-02-26).
ci_summary: All unit and integration checks passed. Initial perf run flagged one flaky regression (synthetic worst-case) -> tuned defaults -> perf suite passed on re-run. Linters and static analysis green. Deployment e2e smoke on staging passed.
notes_for_release: Enabled behind feature flag. Ops: monitor slab_fragmentation_ratio and kernel_switch_rate; rollback by disabling slab_eviction.enabled. See docs/runbooks/slab_eviction_rollout.md for playbook.
safety_and_security_review: no PII changes; KMS/HSM not affected. Security reviewed by platform security during design stage.
performance_regression_risks: Risk: aggressive decay_tau on worst-case synthetic streams can increase kernel switch rate temporarily; mitigated by conservative defaults and canary gating.
